• ✓ I have no money. (positive verb + no) Both are correct and mean the same thing. The key rule: use any with a negative verb, and no with a positive verb. Do not combine two negatives. Avoid the double negative. In standard English, one negative word per clause is enough. ✗ I don’t know nothing. → ✓ I don’t know anything. / ✓ I know nothing. Two negatives logically cancel out, so ✗ I didn’t see nobody literally means you did see somebody. (You may hear double negatives in songs and dialects, but avoid them in standard writing and speech.)

Yes/No Questions A yes/no question can be answered with yes or no. We form it by putting the auxiliary or be in front of the subject. This swap is called inversion.

• ✓ Is she ready? (She is ready. → Is she ready?)

• ✓ Are they coming?

• ✓ Have you finished?

• ✓ Can he swim? For the present and past simple, there is no auxiliary to move, so again we use do-support: place do / does / did before the subject and keep the main verb in its base form.

• ✓ Do you like coffee?

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

• ✓ Does she work here?

• ✓ Did they call? A rising voice is not a question (in standard English). Saying ✗ You like coffee? with a question intonation happens in casual speech, but the standard, correct form uses inversion or do: ✓ Do you like coffee? Teach and write the inverted form.

Yes/No question forms across tenses Tense

Statement

Yes/No question

Present simple

You work here.

Do you work here?

Present simple (be)

She is busy.

Is she busy?

Present continuous

They are eating.

Are they eating?

Past simple

He called.

Did he call?

Past continuous

You were sleeping.

Were you sleeping?

Present perfect

We have met.

Have we met?

Past perfect

She had left.

Had she left?

Future (will)

They will help.

Will they help?

Modal

He can drive.

Can he drive?

Wh- Questions Wh- questions ask for information, not just yes or no. They begin with a question word, followed by the same inversion (or dosupport) as a yes/no question: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + main verb The main question words are who, what, which, whose, where, when, why, how, plus the how family: how much, how many, how long, how often, how old.

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

Question word

Asks about

Example

who

a person

Who did you meet?

what

a thing/idea

What do you want?

which

a choice

Which do you prefer?

whose

possession

Whose car is this?

where

a place

Where did she go?

when

a time

When does it start?

why

a reason

Why are you laughing?

how

a manner

How did they win?

how much

quantity (uncountable)

How much does it cost?

how many

quantity (countable)

How many do you need?

how long

duration

How long have you waited?

how often

frequency

How often do you exercise?

how old

age

How old is your sister?

Subject vs Object Questions This is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — points in English questions. When the wh- word asks about the object of the verb, we use normal inversion / do-support:

• ✓ Who did you see? (you is the subject; who is the object)

• ✓ What did she break?

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

But when the wh- word is itself the subject of the verb, there is no inversion and no do/does/did. The question word simply takes the subject’s place, and the verb is conjugated normally.

• ✓ Who broke the window? (not ✗ Who did break the window?)

• ✓ What happened? (not ✗ What did happen?) Subject questions take NO do/does/did. Compare these carefully: - Subject: ✓ Who wants ice cream? — Object: ✓ Who do you want? - Subject: ✓ What made that noise? — Object: ✓ What did you make? - Subject: ✓ Who called you? — Object: ✓ Who did you call? Ask yourself: who or what is doing the verb? If the wh- word is the doer, it is a subject question — keep it simple, no do.

Questions with Prepositions In everyday English, prepositions usually stay at the end of the question, with the wh- word at the front:

• ✓ What are you looking at?

• ✓ Who did you go with?

• ✓ Where does she come from?

• ✓ What is the meeting about? In very formal English, the preposition can move to the front: With whom did you go? This sounds stiff and old-fashioned in conversation, so prefer the end position for natural speech and most writing.

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

Indirect / Embedded Questions When we put a question inside another sentence — often to be more polite — the word order changes back to that of a statement. There is no inversion and no do/does/did. Direct question

Indirect / embedded question

Where is the station?

Could you tell me where the station is?

What does it mean?

I don’t know what it means.

When did they leave?

Do you remember when they left?

• ✓ Could you tell me where the station is? (not ✗ …where is the station?)

• ✓ I wonder why she didn’t call. (not ✗ …why didn’t she call.) For yes/no questions embedded in a sentence, use if or whether:

• ✓ I wonder if it will rain.

• ✓ Do you know whether the shop is open? Indirect questions use statement order. The most common mistake is keeping the inverted order: ✗ Can you tell me what time is it? → ✓ Can you tell me what time it is? Embedded questions sound much more polite, which is why we use them to ask strangers for help.

Negative Questions A negative question puts not / n’t into the question. We use them to express surprise, or to invite the listener to agree with us.

• Don’t you like it? (surprise: I expected you to like it)

• Isn’t this beautiful? (inviting agreement)

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

• Haven’t we met before? (seeking confirmation) Answering negative questions can be tricky for learners. In English, base your yes or no on the facts, not on the wording of the question:

• Don’t you like coffee? — ✓ Yes, I do. (= I do like it) / ✓ No, I don’t. (= I don’t like it) So yes always goes with a positive fact, and no always goes with a negative fact, regardless of how the question was phrased.

Short Answers and Short Responses We rarely answer with a bare yes or no. Instead, we echo the auxiliary. Use the auxiliary or be from the question — never the full verb.

• Do you like it? — ✓ Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.

• Is she coming? — ✓ Yes, she is. / No, she isn’t.

• Can you drive? — ✓ Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.

• Have they arrived? — ✓ Yes, they have. / No, they haven’t. Don’t repeat the main verb in a short answer. ✗ Do you like it? — Yes, I like. → ✓ Yes, I do. The auxiliary does all the work.

Question Tags A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to check information or invite agreement: It’s cold today, isn’t it?** The rule has three parts:

1. Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

2. Use the same auxiliary (or be) as the statement. If the statement is present/past simple with no auxiliary, use do / does / did.

3. Use a pronoun that matches the subject.

• ✓ She is tired, isn’t she? (positive → negative)

• ✓ She isn’t tired, is she? (negative → positive)

• ✓ You like tea, don’t you? (no auxiliary → do)

• ✓ He went home, didn’t he?

Question tags across tenses Statement

Tag

You’re a teacher,

aren’t you?

She isn’t here,

is she?

They live nearby,

don’t they?

He doesn’t smoke,

does he?

We met before,

didn’t we?

You can swim,

can’t you?

It won’t rain,

will it?

She has left,

hasn’t she?

You wouldn’t lie,

would you?

Special cases A few tags do not follow the basic pattern and must be learned: Statement

Tag

Note

I’m late,

aren’t I?

am I not is too formal; we say aren’t I

Open the window,

will you / won’t you / can you?

imperatives

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

Statement

Tag

Note

Don’t be late,

will you?

negative imperative

Let’s go,

shall we?

suggestions with let’s

There’s a problem,

isn’t there?

there repeats as the subject

Everyone agrees,

don’t they?

everyone / someone / nobody → they

Nobody called,

did they?

nobody is already negative → positive tag

Intonation changes the meaning. A falling voice on the tag means you expect agreement — you are not really asking: Lovely day, isn’t it?↓ A rising voice turns it into a genuine question: You locked the door, didn’t you?↑ (you truly want to know).

So / Neither + Auxiliary + Subject To say that something is also true for someone, use so + auxiliary + subject (for positive statements) or neither / nor + auxiliary + subject (for negative statements). Notice the inversion — the auxiliary comes before the subject.

• I like jazz. — ✓ So do I. (= I like it too)

• She’s tired. — ✓ So am I.

• I can’t swim. — ✓ Neither can I. / ✓ Nor can I.

• He doesn’t eat meat. — ✓ Neither do I. Match the auxiliary, and invert. ✗ So I do. → ✓ So do I. For negatives, do not add a second not: ✗ Neither I don’t. → ✓ Neither do I. (neither already carries the negative meaning).

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

Quick Review

• Negatives, questions, short answers, and tags all run on the auxiliary verb. For the present/past simple, borrow do/does/did and keep the main verb in its base form.

• Yes/no questions invert subject and auxiliary; wh- questions add a question word in front.

• Subject questions (Who broke it?) take no do/does/did and no inversion — this is the key trap.

• Indirect questions use statement word order and are more polite (Could you tell me where it is?).

• Avoid double negatives: use any with a negative verb, no with a positive verb.

• Question tags: opposite polarity, same auxiliary, pronoun subject — with special cases (aren’t I?, shall we?, isn’t there?).

• Use So do I / Neither do I to agree, matching the auxiliary and inverting.

Practice

Rewrite or complete each item correctly.

1. Make negative: She understands the question.

2. Make a yes/no question: They have finished the project.

3. Correct the error: He doesn’t likes vegetables.

4. Subject or object question? Complete: ______ wrote this letter? (the writer is unknown)

5. Make a wh- question asking about the object: You called ______ last night? → (use who)

C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S

6. Turn into an indirect question: Where is the bank? → Could you tell me ______?

7. Add a question tag: You’re coming to the party, ______?

8. Add a question tag: Let’s leave early, ______?

9. Correct the double negative: I didn’t see nobody.

10. Respond showing you agree: “I don’t like horror films.” “______ I.”

Answers

1. She doesn’t understand the question. (base form understand)

2. Have they finished the project?

3. He doesn’t like vegetables. (base form after doesn’t)

4. Who wrote this letter? — a subject question, so no do/did.

5. Who did* you call last night? — an object question, so use did* + base form.

6. Could you tell me where the bank is? (statement order, no inversion)

7. You’re coming to the party, aren’t you?

8. Let’s leave early, shall we?

9. I didn’t see anybody. (or I saw nobody.)

10. “Neither do I.” (or “Nor do I.”)

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

chapters.title: Punctuation, Capitalization & Common Mistakes
chapters.text:
Chapter 25 — Punctuation, Capitalization & Common Mistakes Punctuation and capitalization are the traffic signals of writing. They tell your reader when to pause, when to stop, where one idea ends and another begins, and which words deserve special weight. Get them right and your meaning flows clearly; get them wrong and even good ideas can confuse. This capstone chapter brings together the marks you will use every day, the capitalization rules that catch out even confident writers, and a practical reference to the mistakes and confused words that appear most often. Where British (BrE) and American (AmE) usage differ, we will say so clearly.

Part A — Punctuation The Full Stop / Period, Question Mark, and Exclamation Mark These three marks end sentences. The full stop (BrE) or period (AmE) closes a statement or a command.

• ✓ She lives in Lisbon.

• ✓ Please close the door. The question mark closes a direct question. Do not use it after an indirect (reported) question.

• ✓ Where do you live?

• ✗ I asked where she lived? → ✓ I asked where she lived.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

The exclamation mark signals strong feeling, surprise, or emphasis. Use it sparingly; one is almost always enough.

• ✓ What a beautiful view!

• ✗ Thank you so much!!! → ✓ Thank you so much!

Tip: In formal writing, exclamation marks are rare. If everything is emphasized, nothing is.

The Comma — The Big One The comma is the most useful and the most misused mark in English. It separates parts of a sentence so readers can group ideas correctly. Here are its main jobs.

1. Separating items in a list. Use commas between three or more items.

• ✓ We bought bread, cheese, and olives. The comma before and (or or) in a list is called the serial comma or Oxford comma. It is standard in much American writing and optional in British writing. It can prevent ambiguity.

• ✓ I’d like to thank my parents, Oprah, and God. (three separate things)

• ✗ I’d like to thank my parents, Oprah and God. (could suggest your parents are Oprah and God) BrE vs AmE — the Oxford comma: AmE often uses it by default; BrE often omits it unless needed for clarity. Either is acceptable — just be consistent within a piece of writing.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

2. After an introductory element. Use a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or clause.

• ✓ After the meeting, we went for coffee.

• ✓ Honestly, I had no idea.

• ✓ Because it was raining, the match was cancelled.

3. Around non-essential information. If a phrase or clause adds extra (removable) detail, surround it with commas. If it is essential to the meaning, do not.

• ✓ My brother, who lives in Tokyo, is a chef. (non-essential — I have one brother)

• ✓ The man who lives next door is a chef. (essential — tells us which man) 4.

Before

a

coordinating

conjunction

joining

two

independent clauses. When and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor join two complete sentences, put a comma before the conjunction.

• ✓ I called twice, but no one answered.

• ✓ She studied hard, so she passed easily. Do not add a comma when the conjunction simply joins two verbs (not two full clauses).

• ✗ She studied hard, and passed. → ✓ She studied hard and passed.

5. With direct address and dates. Use a comma to set off the name of the person spoken to, and within dates.

• ✓ Thanks, Maria, for your help.

• ✓ Let’s eat, Grandma. (Without the comma — Let’s eat Grandma — the meaning changes alarmingly.)

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

• ✓ She was born on June 19, 2026, in Berlin. (AmE style; note the comma after the year too)

• ✓ She was born on 19 June 2026 in Berlin. (BrE style usually needs no commas)

⚠️ The Comma Splice — A Common Serious Error A comma splice happens when two complete sentences are joined with only a comma. - ✗ It was late, we went home. You can fix it in one of three ways: 1. Use a full stop: ✓ It was late. We went home. 2. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; we went home. 3. Add a coordinating conjunction: ✓ It was late, so we went home. Note: however, therefore, then, and moreover are not coordinating conjunctions, so a comma before them still creates a splice. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; however, we stayed.

The Semicolon and the Colon The semicolon (;) links two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction. Each side could stand alone as a sentence.

• ✓ The roads were icy; the buses stopped running.

• ✓ Some people love winter; others can’t wait for spring. It also separates list items that already contain commas.

• ✓ The tour visits Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Madrid, Spain. The colon (:) introduces something: a list, an explanation, or an example. What comes before a colon should normally be a complete clause.

• ✓ She had one goal: to finish the marathon.

• ✓ Bring three things: a pen, paper, and an open mind.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

• ✗ Bring: a pen, paper, and an open mind. (the part before the colon is not a full clause) Mark

Use it to…

Example

Semicolon

Join two related complete sentences

I was tired; I kept working.

Colon

Introduce a list, explanation, or result

I had one wish: rest.

The Apostrophe The apostrophe has two main jobs: showing contractions and showing possession. Contractions — the apostrophe marks missing letters.

• ✓ do not → don’t, I am → I’m, they will → they’ll, of the clock → o’clock Possession — add ’s to singular nouns, and just an ‘ to plural nouns already ending in -s. Case

Rule

Example

Singular

add ’s

the girl’s bag

Singular ending in -s

usually add ’s

James’s car (BrE often James’)

Plural ending in -s

add ‘ only

the girls’ bags

Irregular plural

add ’s

the children’s toys, women’s rights

⚠️ Its vs It’s, and Decades - it’s = it is or it has: ✓ It’s raining. / It’s been a long day. - its = belonging to it (no apostrophe):

✓ The dog wagged its tail. - ✗ Its raining. / ✗ The dog wagged it’s tail. - Decades take no apostrophe: ✓ the 1990s, the 80s — ✗ the 1990’s, the 80’s. - Never use an apostrophe to make an ordinary plural: ✗ apple’s for sale → ✓ apples for sale.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

Quotation Marks Quotation marks enclose direct speech and quoted words.

• ✓ “I’ll be there at six,” she said. BrE vs AmE — quotation marks: - AmE typically uses double quotation marks first: He said, “Hello.” - BrE often uses single quotation marks first: He said, ‘Hello.’ - Quotes inside quotes switch to the other style: AmE “She said ‘no’ twice.” / BrE ‘She said “no” twice.’

The bigger difference is where the final period or comma goes.

• AmE: the comma/period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

• ✓ He called it “brilliant.”

• BrE: the comma/period usually goes outside (unless it belongs to the quoted material).

• ✓ He called it ‘brilliant’. Question marks and exclamation marks go inside only if they belong to the quotation: ✓ She asked, “Are you ready?” but ✓ Did he really say “no”?

Hyphen vs Dash The hyphen (-) is short. It joins words, especially compound modifiers before a noun, and links some prefixes.

• ✓ a well-known author, a five-year-old child, a part-time job

• Note: do not hyphenate when the words come after the noun: ✓ The author is well known.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

A dash is longer and separates, rather than joins.

• The en dash (–) marks ranges: ✓ pages 10–20, the 2010–2020 period.

• The em dash (—) marks a strong break or aside: ✓ She paused — just for a moment — and smiled.

Tip: A hyphen joins; a dash interrupts. They are different lengths and different jobs.

Parentheses Parentheses ( ) — called round brackets in BrE — enclose extra, non-essential information. The sentence should still read correctly if you remove them.

• ✓ The museum (founded in 1880) is free on Sundays.

• ✓ Call me later (after lunch is best). Punctuation belonging to the whole sentence goes outside the closing parenthesis: ✓ We met in Rome (in spring).

Capitalization Capitalize the following: Capitalize

Example

The first word of a sentence

✓ The sun rose.

The pronoun I

✓ Yesterday I left early.

People’s names

✓ Anna Smith

Places

✓ Paris, the Nile, Asia

Nationalities, languages

✓ Spanish food, she speaks Arabic

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

Capitalize

Example

Days and months

✓ Monday, October

Titles of works (main words)

✓ The Lord of the Rings

Titles before a name

✓ President Lincoln, Doctor Patel

Holidays, brands, organizations

✓ Ramadan, Sony, the United Nations

Do not capitalize:

• Seasons: ✗ I love Summer. → ✓ I love summer.

• General directions: ✓ Drive south for an hour. (but capitalize regions: ✓ the South of the country)

• Titles used generally: ✓ She wants to be a doctor. (vs ✓ Doctor Patel)

• Common nouns after a brand or place: ✓ French fries but

✓ a french press is often lowercased; ✓ English grammar (language stays capitalized).

• ✓ On Tuesday, I met a French teacher in March.

• ✗ on tuesday, i met a french Teacher in march.

Part B — Common Mistakes & Confused Pairs This section is a quick reference. For each pair, you get the confusion, the rule, and a ✓/✗ example.

Confused Word Pairs Words

Rule

Example

its / it’s

its = possessive; it’s = it is/ has

✓ It’s lost its shine.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

Words

Rule

Example

your / you’re

your = possessive; you’re = you are

✓ You’re losing your keys.

their / there / they’re

possession / place / they are

✓ They’re putting their bags over there.

whose / who’s

whose = possessive; who’s = who is/has

✓ Who’s the man whose car is blocked?

to / too / two

direction-or-infinitive / alsoor-excess / the number 2

✓ I want to go too, with my two friends.

then / than

then = time; than = comparison

✓ She’s taller than me; back then she was shorter.

affect / effect

affect = verb (to influence); effect = noun (a result)

✓ The noise affected me; it had a real effect.

fewer / less

fewer = countable; less = uncountable

✓ Fewer cars, less traffic.

lie / lay

lie = recline (no object); lay = put down (needs object)

✓ I lie down; I lay the book on the table.

who / whom

who = subject; whom = object

✓ Who called? / To whom did you speak?

e.g. / i.e.

e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is

✓ fruit, e.g. apples / ✓ citrus fruit, i.e. lemons and limes

advice / advise

advice = noun; advise = verb

✓ I advise you to take my advice.

practice / practise

BrE: practice = noun, practise = verb (AmE: practice for both)

✓ I practise daily. (BrE verb) /

✓ good practice

lose / loose

lose = misplace/not win; loose = not tight

✓ Don’t lose the loose screw.

accept / except

accept = receive; except = apart from

✓ Everyone accepted except me.

principal / principle

principal = main / head of school; principle = a rule or belief

✓ The principal acted on principle.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

Words

Rule

Example

stationary / stationery

stationary = not moving; stationery = paper goods

✓ The van was stationary; I bought stationery.

complement / compliment

complement = completes; compliment = praise

✓ The wine complements the meal; she paid me a compliment.

everyday / every day

everyday = ordinary (adjective); every day = each day

✓ an everyday task / ✓ I exercise every day.

into / in to

into = movement/transformation; in to = two words

✓ She walked into the room. / ✓ He came in to help.

Quick check for who/whom: If you can answer the question with he/she/they, use who. If you’d answer with him/her/them, use whom. ✓ Whom did you see? — I saw him.

Subject–Verb Agreement Traps These constructions trip up even advanced learners. Pattern

Rule

Example

everyone / everybody / each / no one

always singular

✓ Everyone is here. (✗ are)

the number of

takes a singular verb

✓ The number of students is rising.

a number of

takes a plural verb

✓ A number of students are absent.

neither / either (alone)

singular

✓ Neither answer is correct.

neither… nor / either… or

verb agrees with the nearer subject

✓ Neither the boys nor the teacher was late. / ✓ Neither the teacher nor the boys were late.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

Pattern

Rule

Example

collective nouns (team, family, government)

AmE usually singular; BrE may use plural

AmE ✓ The team is winning. / BrE

✓ The team are winning.

Other Frequent Learner Errors Error

Why it’s wrong

Correction

✗ I don’t know nothing.

double negative

✓ I don’t know anything.

✗ could of / should of / would of

“of” misheard for “have”

✓ could have, should have, would have

✗ more better / most easiest

double comparative/ superlative

✓ better, easiest

✗ very unique / quite perfect

unique and perfect are absolutes

✓ unique, perfect (or almost unique)

✗ apple’s for sale

apostrophe on a plain plural

✓ apples for sale

✗ I can’t hardly see.

hardly is already negative

✓ I can hardly see.

⚠️ The “could of” trap: In speech, could have sounds like could of (the contraction is could’ve). In writing, always use have: ✓ You could have told me. — ✗ You could of told me.

Quick Review

• End statements with a full stop/period, questions with a question mark, and strong feeling with a single exclamation mark.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

• The comma separates list items, follows introductory elements, brackets non-essential information, and precedes a coordinating conjunction joining two clauses.

• A comma splice joins two sentences with only a comma — fix it with a full stop, a semicolon, or a conjunction.

• The semicolon links related independent clauses; the colon introduces a list, explanation, or result.

• The apostrophe marks contractions and possession — but its is possessive, it’s means it is, and decades (1990s) take no apostrophe.

• Quotation marks: AmE prefers double and puts commas/periods inside; BrE often prefers single and puts them outside.

• A hyphen joins (compound modifiers); a dash interrupts; the en dash marks ranges.

• Capitalize sentence starts, I, proper nouns, nationalities, languages, days, months, and titles — but not seasons.

• Watch the confused pairs (your/you’re, their/there/they’re, affect/effect, fewer/less) and avoid could of, double negatives, and very unique.

Practice

Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.

1. Its been raining all day, and the streets are flooded.

2. We invited two clowns, a magician and a juggler.

3. The meeting was long we left early.

4. My sister who is a doctor lives in canada.

5. You should of called me yesterday.

C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

6. There going to bring they’re books to the library over their.

7. I love the cold weather in Winter.

8. Less people came to the second show than to the first.

9. Each of the students have submitted their essay.

10. James asked, “where are you going”?

Answers

1. ✓ It’s been raining all day, and the streets are flooded. (it’s = it has)

2. ✓ We invited two clowns, a magician, and a juggler. (serial/Oxford comma clarifies separate acts; in BrE the comma is optional but helpful here)

3. ✓ The meeting was long, so we left early. (comma splice fixed — also valid: …long; we left early. or …long. We left early.)

4. ✓ My sister, who is a doctor, lives in Canada. (non-essential clause needs commas; Canada is a proper noun)

5. ✓ You should have called me yesterday. (should of → should have)

6. ✓ They’re going to bring their books to the library over there. (they are / possessive / place)

7. ✓ I love the cold weather in winter. (seasons are not capitalized)

8. ✓ Fewer people came to the second show than to the first. (people is countable → fewer)

9. ✓ Each of the students has submitted his or her essay. (each is singular → has; their is widely accepted, but the verb must be has)

10. ✓ James asked, “Where are you going?” (capital after the quotation opens; the question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside, in both AmE and BrE)

examples.t: I walk to work every day.

exercises.q: Water ______ (freeze) at 0 °C.
exercises.answer: freezes — present simple; a general scientific truth

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: I ______ (live) in this city since 2015.
exercises.answer: have lived (or have been living) — present perfect; a state continuing to now with since

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: When the alarm went off, we ______ (sleep).
exercises.answer: were sleeping — past continuous; background action in progress when interrupted

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: By next year, they ______ (be) married for a decade.
exercises.answer: will have been — future perfect; completed state by a future point (By next year)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: She ______ (write) emails all morning, so her hand hurts.
exercises.answer: has been writing — present perfect continuous; duration of an activity with a present result

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: I _____ that film — let’s watch something else.
exercises.answer: have already seen — present perfect; experience linked to now (British usage especially). American English may also accept already saw

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: We ______ (visit) my grandmother last Sunday.
exercises.answer: visited — past simple; a finished event at a stated past time (last Sunday)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: As soon as I ______ (finish) this report, I’ll send it to you.
exercises.answer: finish — present simple for future meaning after the time word as soon as

exercises.instr: Choose the correct tense for each gap. (Some have more than one good answer; pick the most natural.)
exercises.q: The clouds are dark — it ______ (rain).
exercises.answer: is going to rain — going to for a prediction based on present evidence

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: ✗ She cans play the violin. — Correct the sentence.
exercises.answer: She can play the violin. (no -s on a modal)

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: When the alarm rang, the staff _____ evacuate the building safely.
exercises.answer: were able to — a single, specific past success

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: You _____ tell her — it’s meant to be a surprise!
exercises.answer: mustn’t — it is forbidden (to spoil the surprise)

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: It’s a holiday tomorrow, so we _____ get up early.
exercises.answer: don’t have to — there is no obligation; getting up early is optional

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: His car isn’t in the drive. He _____ have gone out.
exercises.answer: must — a logical positive deduction (the missing car is the evidence)

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: I’m exhausted. I _____ have stayed up so late last night.
exercises.answer: shouldn’t — regret about something you actually did

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: Choose the more polite request: (a) Can you help me? (b) Could you help me?
exercises.answer: (b) Could you help me? is more polite than Can you…?

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: You _____ brought a gift — but thank you, it was kind of you. (The gift was brought.)
exercises.answer: needn’t have — the gift was brought, but it was unnecessary

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: Rewrite using a modal substitute: “She will ______ come to the party.” (ability)
exercises.answer: She will be able to come to the party. (be able to substitutes for can after will)

exercises.instr: Choose or complete the correct form.
exercises.q: Winters in the mountains _____ be extremely cold — it happens every year.
exercises.answer: can — general possibility (a regular, recurring fact)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make passive: Someone has stolen my wallet.
exercises.answer: My wallet has been stolen

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make passive: They are building a new hospital.
exercises.answer: A new hospital is being built

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make passive: The teacher will correct the tests.
exercises.answer: The tests will be corrected (by the teacher)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make passive (two ways): They offered Maria a scholarship.
exercises.answer: Maria was offered a scholarship. / A scholarship was offered to Maria

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Correct the error: The letter was wrote yesterday.
exercises.answer: The letter was written yesterday. (past participle, not wrote)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Correct the error: The earthquake was happened at midnight.
exercises.answer: The earthquake happened at midnight. (happen is intransitive — no passive)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make active: The thief was seen by a neighbour.
exercises.answer: A neighbour saw the thief

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Complete with the passive infinitive: These documents need ______ (sign) today.
exercises.answer: These documents need to be signed today

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Rewrite using “He is said to…”: People say that he lives in Paris.
exercises.answer: He is said to live in Paris

exercises.instr: Rewrite or correct as instructed.
exercises.q: Make passive (modal): You must wash the dishes.
exercises.answer: The dishes must be washed

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: If you __ (mix) blue and yellow, you ____ (get) green.
exercises.answer: mix … get (zero conditional — a general truth)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: If it __ (be) sunny tomorrow, we ____ (have) a picnic.
exercises.answer: is … will have (first conditional — real future; note the present is in the if-clause)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: If I ______ (be) you, I wouldn’t trust him.
exercises.answer: were (If I were you — were for all persons)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: If she __ (study) harder last year, she ____ (pass) the exam.
exercises.answer: had studied … would have passed (third conditional — unreal past)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: I wish I ______ (know) how to swim. (regret about now)
exercises.answer: knew (wish + past simple for a present regret)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: Rewrite without if, using inversion: If I had seen the sign, I would have stopped.
exercises.answer: Had I seen the sign, I would have stopped. (inversion; no if, no comma after Had)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: Choose the correct word: I won’t lend you the car (unless / as long as) you don’t drive too fast.
exercises.answer: as long as — I won’t lend you the car as long as you don’t drive too fast. (Unless you don’t would create a double negative; the natural alternative would be unless you drive too fast.)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: Correct the mistake: If it will snow, we will build a snowman.
exercises.answer: If it snows, we will build a snowman. (remove will from the if-clause)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: Make a mixed conditional: past condition, present result — I didn’t learn French. I can’t read this menu now.
exercises.answer: If I had learned French, I would be able to read this menu now. (past condition → present result)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct form.
exercises.q: Complete: It’s high time you ______ (clean) your room.
exercises.answer: cleaned (It’s high time + past simple)

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “I am learning Spanish,” she said.
exercises.answer: She said (that) she was learning Spanish

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “We have finished the project,” they told me.
exercises.answer: They told me (that) they had finished the project

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “I will email you tomorrow,” he said. (reporting on a different day)
exercises.answer: He said (that) he would email me the next day

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “Where do you work?” she asked me.
exercises.answer: She asked me where I worked

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “Are you feeling better?” the nurse asked him.
exercises.answer: The nurse asked him if/whether he was feeling better

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “Close the door,” the teacher told us.
exercises.answer: The teacher told us to close the door

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “Don’t worry about the exam,” she told me.
exercises.answer: She told me not to worry about the exam

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “I’ll help you carry the bags,” he said. (use offer)
exercises.answer: He offered to help me carry the bags

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “No, I won’t sign it,” she said. (use refuse)
exercises.answer: She refused to sign it

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence in reported speech. Use a past reporting verb and backshift where appropriate.
exercises.q: “Let’s go to the beach,” he said. (use suggest)
exercises.answer: He suggested going to the beach. (also correct: He suggested that we go to the beach.)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: I really enjoy ______ (read) before bed.
exercises.answer: reading — enjoy is always followed by the gerund

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: She decided ______ (study) medicine.
exercises.answer: to study — decide takes the to-infinitive

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: Remember ______ (post) the letter on your way out — it’s urgent.
exercises.answer: to post — remember to do means a duty you must not forget (the letter is not yet posted)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: He’s very good at ______ (play) the guitar.
exercises.answer: playing — after the preposition at, use the gerund

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: They let their children ______ (stay) up late on Fridays.
exercises.answer: stay — let + object takes the bare infinitive (no to)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: I came here ______ (ask) you a question.
exercises.answer: to ask — the to-infinitive of purpose: it explains why he came

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: We can’t afford ______ (eat) out every night.
exercises.answer: to eat — afford takes the to-infinitive

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: Do you mind ______ (close) the door?
exercises.answer: closing — mind is followed by the gerund

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: I’ll never forget ______ (see) the Grand Canyon for the first time.
exercises.answer: seeing — forget doing refers to a memory you will always keep

exercises.instr: Choose the correct form (gerund or infinitive) of the verb in brackets. Some items have two acceptable answers — explain the meaning where it matters.
exercises.q: You’d better ______ (leave) now if you want to catch the train.
exercises.answer: leave — after had better, use the bare infinitive

exercises.instr: Identify the type (1 = intransitive, 2 = separable, 3 = inseparable, 4 = three-part).
exercises.q: My computer broke down this morning.
exercises.answer: 1 — intransitive (no object; break down = stop working)

exercises.instr: Identify the type (1 = intransitive, 2 = separable, 3 = inseparable, 4 = three-part).
exercises.q: Please turn off the television.
exercises.answer: 2 — separable (you can also say turn the television off / turn it off)

exercises.instr: Identify the type (1 = intransitive, 2 = separable, 3 = inseparable, 4 = three-part).
exercises.q: She looks after her elderly neighbour.
exercises.answer: 3 — inseparable (look after the neighbour / look after her; never look her after)

exercises.instr: Identify the type (1 = intransitive, 2 = separable, 3 = inseparable, 4 = three-part).
exercises.q: We’re looking forward to the concert.
exercises.answer: 4 — three-part (look forward to + noun/-ing)

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence, replacing the underlined object with a pronoun.
exercises.q: Can you turn off the lights?
exercises.answer: Can you turn them off? (pronoun in the middle; ✗ turn off them)

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence, replacing the underlined object with a pronoun.
exercises.q: He threw away the newspaper.
exercises.answer: He threw it away. (✗ threw away it)

exercises.instr: Rewrite each sentence, replacing the underlined object with a pronoun.
exercises.q: She looks after the children.
exercises.answer: She looks after them. (inseparable, so the pronoun stays after the particle; ✗ looks them after)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct particle.
exercises.q: I need to find ___ when the shop opens.
exercises.answer: out — find out = discover

exercises.instr: Choose the correct particle.
exercises.q: They don’t get ___ with their landlord.
exercises.answer: on — get on with = have a good relationship

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake.
exercises.q: I look forward to meet you next week.
exercises.answer: I look forward to meeting you next week. (to is a preposition, so use the -ing form.) PART IV Describing & Connecting Adjectives, adverbs, comparison, prepositions, conjunctions, and relative clauses — the tools that add detail and join ideas

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: The film was really _____.
exercises.answer: boring (the film causes the feeling)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: She plays the piano _____.
exercises.answer: well (adverb describing how she plays)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: They live in a _____ cottage.
exercises.answer: small old (size before age)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: I’m _____ exhausted after the marathon.
exercises.answer: absolutely (exhausted is non-gradable)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: He _____ ever eats meat.
exercises.answer: hardly (hardly ever = almost never)

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
exercises.q: We bought two reds bicycles.
exercises.answer: We bought two red bicycles. (adjectives take no plural -s)

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
exercises.q: I am very interesting in history.
exercises.answer: I am very interested in history. (a feeling → -ed)

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
exercises.q: She smiled at me friendlily.
exercises.answer: She smiled at me in a friendly way. (friendly has no -ly adverb)

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
exercises.q: He walks usually to the office.
exercises.answer: He usually walks to the office. (frequency adverb before the main verb)

exercises.instr: Correct the mistake in each sentence.
exercises.q: That dress is very perfect.
exercises.answer: That dress is absolutely perfect. (perfect is non-gradable; not very)

exercises.instr: Put the adverbs in the correct order.
exercises.q: She danced (last night / gracefully / at the party).
exercises.answer: She danced gracefully at the party last night. (manner–place– time)

exercises.instr: Put the adverbs in the correct order.
exercises.q: I have (been / never / to Japan).
exercises.answer: I have never been to Japan. (frequency adverb after the auxiliary) C H A P T E R 2 0 — C O M PA R AT I V E S & S U P E R L AT I V E S

exercises.q: Write the comparative and superlative of each word. a) easy b) expensive c) good d) thin e) far
exercises.answer: a) easier / the easiest b) more expensive / the most expensive c) better / the best d) thinner / the thinnest e) farther (further) / the farthest (furthest)

exercises.q: Choose the correct form. a) Mount Fuji is _____ than that hill. b) This is the (more / most) exciting book I’ve read this year. c) Today is (hot / hotter / hottest) than yesterday.
exercises.answer: a) higher b) most c) hotter

exercises.q: Correct the mistake in each sentence. a) My phone is more cheaper than yours. b) He is very taller than his father. c) She sings better then me.
exercises.answer: a) My phone is cheaper than yours. (remove more) b) He is much taller than his father. (very → much) c) She sings better than me. (then → than)

exercises.q: Complete with as … as, not as … as, or than. a) A bicycle isn’t ___ fast ___ a car. b) This café is busier ___ the one next door. c) Your bag is exactly ___ heavy ___ mine — we packed the same amount.
exercises.answer: a) not as … as — A bicycle isn’t as fast as a car. b) than — busier than the one next door. c) as … as — exactly as heavy as mine

exercises.q: Fill the gap with much, a bit, or slightly (more than one answer may fit). a) Don’t worry, it’s only ___ colder than yesterday. b) C H A P T E R 2 0 — C O M PA R AT I V E S & S U P E R L AT I V E S Their new house is ___ bigger than the old one — almost double the size!
exercises.answer: a) a bit or slightly b) much

exercises.q: Complete the the + comparative sentences. a) The more you sleep, the ___ (good) you feel. b) The ___ (soon) we start, the ___ (soon) we finish.
exercises.answer: a) better b) sooner … sooner

exercises.q: Choose fewer or less. a) I made (fewer / less) mistakes this time. b) We have (fewer / less) money than last month.
exercises.answer: a) fewer b) less

exercises.q: Rewrite using a superlative + present perfect. Example: I have never seen such a beautiful sunset. → It’s the most beautiful sunset I’ve ever seen. a) I have never read such a boring book. b) We have never had such a good holiday.
exercises.answer: a) It’s the most boring book I’ve ever read. b) It’s the best holiday we’ve ever had

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: The lesson begins _ 9 o’clock _ Monday morning.
exercises.answer: at 9 o’clock on Monday morning. (clock time → at; day → on)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: She has lived in this city ____ 2015.
exercises.answer: since 2015. (a starting point → since)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: Are you afraid ____ the dark?
exercises.answer: afraid of the dark. (dependent preposition)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: We must finish the report ____ Friday at the latest.
exercises.answer: by Friday. (a deadline → by)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: They ____ (discuss) the problem for an hour. (verb + preposition or —?)
exercises.answer: They discussed the problem (—, no preposition). ✗ discussed about

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: The plane _ (arrive) _ New York at noon.
exercises.answer: The plane arrived in New York. (arrive in + city; never arrive to)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: I’m not very good ____ remembering names.
exercises.answer: good at remembering names. (good at + -ing)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: ____ the end, we decided to take the earlier train.
exercises.answer: In the end, we decided… (eventually → in the end)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: He’s married ____ a famous musician.
exercises.answer: married to a famous musician. (✗ married with)

exercises.instr: Choose or supply the correct preposition. (Where a verb needs no preposition, write —.)
exercises.q: Please don’t stand ____ the way; people are trying to pass.
exercises.answer: in the way. (blocking → in the way)

exercises.instr: Add a comma where one is needed (or write “no comma”).
exercises.q: The road was icy so we drove slowly.
exercises.answer: The road was icy, so we drove slowly. (two clauses + FANBOYS)

exercises.instr: Add a comma where one is needed (or write “no comma”).
exercises.q: She opened the laptop and started to type.
exercises.answer: No comma. (one subject she, two verbs)

exercises.instr: Add a comma where one is needed (or write “no comma”).
exercises.q: Although the test was hard everyone passed.
exercises.answer: Although the test was hard, everyone passed. (subordinate clause first)

exercises.instr: Add a comma where one is needed (or write “no comma”).
exercises.q: We can eat now or we can wait for Tom.
exercises.answer: We can eat now, or we can wait for Tom. (two clauses + FAN BOYS)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: (Despite / Although) the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
exercises.answer: Although — followed by a clause (the heavy traffic alone would need despite; here the sentence has a noun phrase, so Despite is also acceptable: Despite the heavy traffic). Best single answer for a clause: if the original read the heavy traffic, choose Despite. → Despite the heavy traffic, we arrived on time

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: The flight was delayed (because / because of) the storm.
exercises.answer: because of — followed by the noun the storm

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: It was _____ a wonderful concert that nobody wanted to leave.
exercises.answer: such — followed by a wonderful concert (a/an + noun)

exercises.instr: Choose the correct word.
exercises.q: Neither the players nor the coach _____ happy with the result.
exercises.answer: was — the nearer subject is the coach (singular)

exercises.instr: Fix the comma splice or run-on.
exercises.q: The shop was closed, we went home.
exercises.answer: The shop was closed, so we went home. (or …closed. We went home. / …closed; we went home.)

exercises.instr: Fix the comma splice or run-on.
exercises.q: He trained for months therefore he won easily.
exercises.answer: He trained for months; therefore, he won easily. (or …months. Therefore, he won easily.)

exercises.instr: Combine each pair using the word in brackets.
exercises.q: It was raining. We played outside. (although)
exercises.answer: Although it was raining, we played outside

exercises.instr: Combine each pair using the word in brackets.
exercises.q: She was nervous. She gave a great speech. (despite)
exercises.answer: Despite being nervous, she gave a great speech. (or Despite her nervousness, she gave a great speech.)

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Fill the gap: The woman _____ won the race is my neighbour.
exercises.answer: who — who refers to a person (the woman)

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Fill the gap: This is the museum _____ the painting is kept.
exercises.answer: where — it refers to a place (the museum)

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Add commas if needed: My grandmother who is eighty-five still drives. (assume only one grandmother)
exercises.answer: My grandmother, who is eighty-five, still drives. — With only one grandmother, the clause is non-defining, so commas are needed

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Can the pronoun be omitted? The film that was released yesterday is a hit. (yes / no — why?)
exercises.answer: No. That is the subject of the clause (followed by the verb was released); subject pronouns can never be omitted

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Correct the error: The boy what broke the window ran away.
exercises.answer: The boy who / that broke the window ran away. — What cannot be used as a relative pronoun here

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Correct the error: London, that is the capital of England, is huge.
exercises.answer: London, which is the capital of England, is huge. — That is not allowed in a non-defining (comma) clause

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Make it formal (front-position preposition): The colleague who I work with is helpful.
exercises.answer: The colleague with whom I work is helpful

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Combine using which (referring to the whole idea): She passed all her exams. This made her parents proud.
exercises.answer: She passed all her exams, which made her parents proud

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Reduce the clause to a participle: The students who are waiting outside can come in now.
exercises.answer: The students waiting outside can come in now

exercises.instr: Complete or correct each sentence.
exercises.q: Correct the error: The man who he called me was very polite.
exercises.answer: The man who called me was very polite. — Remove the double subject he. exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Make negative: She understands the question.
exercises.answer: She doesn’t understand the question. (base form understand)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Make a yes/no question: They have finished the project.
exercises.answer: Have they finished the project?

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Correct the error: He doesn’t likes vegetables.
exercises.answer: He doesn’t like vegetables. (base form after doesn’t)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Subject or object question? Complete: ______ wrote this letter? (the writer is unknown)
exercises.answer: Who wrote this letter? — a subject question, so no do/did

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Make a wh- question asking about the object: You called ______ last night? → (use who) C H A P T E R 2 4 — Q U E S T I O N S , N E G AT I V E S & Q U E S T I O N TA G S
exercises.answer: Who did* you call last night? — an object question, so use did* + base form

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Turn into an indirect question: Where is the bank? → Could you tell me ______?
exercises.answer: Could you tell me where the bank is? (statement order, no inversion)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Add a question tag: You’re coming to the party, ______?
exercises.answer: You’re coming to the party, aren’t you?

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Add a question tag: Let’s leave early, ______?
exercises.answer: Let’s leave early, shall we?

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Correct the double negative: I didn’t see nobody.
exercises.answer: I didn’t see anybody. (or I saw nobody.)

exercises.instr: Rewrite or complete each item correctly.
exercises.q: Respond showing you agree: “I don’t like horror films.” “______ I.”
exercises.answer: “Neither do I.” (or “Nor do I.”) C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: Its been raining all day, and the streets are flooded.
exercises.answer: ✓ It’s been raining all day, and the streets are flooded. (it’s = it has)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: We invited two clowns, a magician and a juggler.
exercises.answer: ✓ We invited two clowns, a magician, and a juggler. (serial/Oxford comma clarifies separate acts; in BrE the comma is optional but helpful here)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: The meeting was long we left early.
exercises.answer: ✓ The meeting was long, so we left early. (comma splice fixed — also valid: …long; we left early. or …long. We left early.)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: My sister who is a doctor lives in canada.
exercises.answer: ✓ My sister, who is a doctor, lives in Canada. (non-essential clause needs commas; Canada is a proper noun)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: You should of called me yesterday. C H A P T E R 2 5 — P U N C T U AT I O N , C A P I TA L I Z AT I O N & C O M M O N M I S TA K E S
exercises.answer: ✓ You should have called me yesterday. (should of → should have)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: There going to bring they’re books to the library over their.
exercises.answer: ✓ They’re going to bring their books to the library over there. (they are / possessive / place)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: I love the cold weather in Winter.
exercises.answer: ✓ I love the cold weather in winter. (seasons are not capitalized)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: Less people came to the second show than to the first.
exercises.answer: ✓ Fewer people came to the second show than to the first. (people is countable → fewer)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: Each of the students have submitted their essay.
exercises.answer: ✓ Each of the students has submitted his or her essay. (each is singular → has; their is widely accepted, but the verb must be has)

exercises.instr: Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.
exercises.q: James asked, “where are you going”?
exercises.answer: ✓ James asked, “Where are you going?” (capital after the quotation opens; the question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside, in both AmE and BrE)

glossary.def: The form of a sentence in which the subject performs the action of the verb; it contrasts with the passive voice. The dog chased the cat.
A word that describes or modifies a noun or pronoun, giving information about qualities such as size, colour, or number. a tall building.
A word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb, or a whole sentence, often expressing manner, place, time, frequency, or degree. Many end in -ly. She sang beautifully.
A word, phrase, or clause that functions the way an adverb does, adding information about how, when, where, or why. He left in a hurry.
The matching of grammatical forms so that related words share features such as number and person, most often a verb agreeing with its subject. She walks; they walk.
The noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers back to. Maria lost her keys, but she found them later. (Maria is the antecedent of she.)
The punctuation mark (’) used to show possession or to mark omitted letters in a contraction. the dog’s bone; don’t.
A word placed before a noun to show whether it is specific or general. English has the definite article the and the indefinite articles a and an. See also zero article.

The grammatical category that shows how an action relates to the flow of time, such as whether it is in progress or completed. English has two main aspects, the continuous (progressive) and the perfect. She is reading; she has read.
A “helping” verb used with a main verb to form tenses, questions, negatives, or the passive. The primary auxiliaries are be, do, and have. She is working; do you know? See also modal verb.
The infinitive used without the word to, appearing after modal verbs and certain other verbs. You should go; let me help.

A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb. A main (independent) clause can stand alone; a subordinate (dependent) clause cannot and depends on a main clause. I stayed home because it was raining.
A noun that refers to a group of people or things as a single unit: team, family, committee, flock. It can take a singular or plural verb depending on the meaning.
The form of an adjective or adverb used to compare two things, formed with -er or more. taller, more carefully. See also superlative.
A word or phrase that completes the meaning of a verb, often describing the subject or object. She is a doctor; the soup tastes delicious.
A noun made up of two or more words acting as a single unit. toothbrush, swimming pool, mother-in-law.
A structure (often using if) that expresses that one thing depends on another, describing possible or imagined situations. If it rains, we will stay in.
The verb aspect formed with be + the -ing participle, showing an action in progress. They are watching television.
A shortened form in which two words are combined and missing letters are marked by an apostrophe. don’t (do not), she’s (she is), we’ll (we will).
A conjunction that joins words, phrases, or clauses of equal grammatical rank: and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet. I tried, but I failed.
A noun naming something that can be counted and that has both singular and plural forms. one book, two books. Contrast with uncountable noun.
A modifying phrase that does not logically attach to the word it is meant to describe, often because that word is missing. Walking to school, the rain began to fall. (The rain was not walking.)
The word the, used before a noun to refer to something specific or already known. Please pass the salt.
A word that points to something and shows whether it is near or far: this, that, these, those. This* is mine; those* are yours.
Another name for a subordinate clause: a clause that cannot stand alone and relies on a main clause. …although she was tired.
A word placed before a noun to identify or quantify it, such as an article, demonstrative, possessive, or quantifier. the, this, my, some, every.
The noun or pronoun that receives the action of a transitive verb. She read a book.
Reporting words by quoting them exactly, usually within quotation marks. He said, “I am leaving now.” Contrast with indirect (reported) speech.
The omission of words that can be understood from the context. She can sing and (she can) dance. The term also names the punctuation mark (…) that shows omitted text.
A verb form that shows tense, person, and number and can serve as the main verb of a clause. She writes; they wrote. Contrast with non-finite forms (infinitives, participles).
The category showing who is involved: the first person is the speaker (I, we), the second person the listener (you), and the third person the one spoken about (he, she, it, they).
The -ing form of a verb used as a noun. Swimming* is good exercise; I enjoy reading*.

An adjective describing a quality that can exist in different degrees, so it can be used with words like very or in comparative forms. cold, colder, very cold. Contrast with non-gradable adjectives like perfect.
The verb form used to give commands, instructions, or requests, usually with no stated subject. Close* the door; be* careful.
The words a and an, used before a singular countable noun to refer to something non-specific. I saw a dog and an owl.
A clause containing a subject and a finite verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence; also called a main clause. The sun rose.
The person or thing that receives the direct object, often answering “to whom?” or “for whom?”. She gave him a gift.
Reporting what someone said without quoting the exact words, usually with changes to tense and pronouns. He said (that) he was leaving. Contrast with direct speech.
The base form of a verb, usually preceded by to. I want to learn. See also bare infinitive.
A change in the form of a word to express grammatical meaning such as tense, number, or comparison. walk → walked; cat → cats.
A verb that does not take a direct object. She slept. Contrast with transitive verb.
A verb that does not form its past tense and past participle with the regular -ed ending. go → went → gone.
A verb that connects the subject to a complement that describes or identifies it, rather than showing an action: be, seem, become, appear, feel. He seems tired.
The verb in a clause that carries the principal meaning, as opposed to an auxiliary. She has finished. (Finished is the main verb; has is the auxiliary.)
An auxiliary verb expressing meanings such as ability, possibility, permission, obligation, or advice: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would. You must wait; she can swim.
A word or group of words that describes or limits another element in a sentence. Adjectives and adverbs are common modifiers. a bright light.

The grammatical category that shows the speaker’s attitude toward what is said: stating a fact (indicative), giving a command (imperative), or expressing a wish or hypothesis (subjunctive). He goes; Go!; I wish he were here.
A word, form, or structure that expresses denial or absence, typically using not or words like no, never, nobody. She does not know.
A relative clause that adds extra, non-essential information about a noun and is set off by commas; removing it does not change the basic meaning. My brother, who lives in Rome, is a chef.
A word that names a person, place, thing, idea, or quality. teacher, London, table, freedom.
A noun together with the words that modify it, functioning as a single unit in a sentence. the tall man in the grey coat.

A noun, pronoun, or noun phrase affected by the action of a verb or governed by a preposition. It may be a direct object, an indirect object, or the object of a preposition. She kicked the ball. Participle (present/past) — A verb form used in compound tenses, in the passive, or as an adjective. The present participle ends in -ing (running); the past participle usually ends in -ed or is irregular (walked, broken). Particle — A short word, often resembling a preposition or adverb, that combines with a verb to form a phrasal verb. give up, look after, turn off.
The form in which the subject receives the action rather than performing it, formed with be + past participle. The cat was chased by the dog. Contrast with active voice.
The verb form used to refer to actions or states in the past. She walked home; they were happy.
The verb aspect formed with have + past participle, linking an earlier action to a later point in time. I have finished.
A verb combined with one or more particles whose meaning often differs from the separate words. give up (stop), look after (care for), put off (postpone).
A group of words working together as a unit but, unlike a clause, not containing both a subject and a finite verb. in the morning; the old house.
The grammatical form indicating more than one. books, children, women. Contrast with singular.
A form showing ownership or a close relationship, made with an apostrophe and s or with a possessive word. Tom’s car; my, your, mine, hers.
The part of a clause that says something about the subject, containing the verb and any objects, complements, or adverbials. The children played in the garden.
A group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning. un-happy, re-write. See also suffix.
A word that shows the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word, often expressing position, direction, or time: in, on, at, under, before, between. The cat is under the table.
A preposition together with its object and any modifiers, working as a unit. on the table; after a long day; in the morning.
The verb form used to refer to current actions, habits, general truths, or states. She works here; water boils at 100°C.
A word used in place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid repetition: I, you, he, she, it, they, who, this, mine. Maria called and she sounded happy.
A noun naming a particular person, place, or organisation, normally written with a capital letter. London, Sarah, Microsoft, Monday.
A determiner or phrase expressing quantity without an exact number: some, many, much, few, several, a lot of. Many people came.
A short question added to the end of a statement, usually to invite agreement or confirmation. You’re coming, aren’t you? She didn’t call, did she?
A pronoun ending in -self or -selves that refers back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, themselves. She taught herself to paint.
The level of formality and style of language chosen to suit a situation, audience, or purpose. Formal: “I would be grateful if you could…”; informal: “Can you…?”
A verb that forms its past tense and past participle by adding -ed to the base form. walk → walked. Contrast with irregular verb.
A clause that gives more information about a noun, usually introduced by a relative pronoun. The man who lives next door is a doctor. See also non-defining relative clause.
A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to a noun: who, whom, whose, which, that. the book that I read.
Another name for indirect speech: reporting what was said without quoting the exact words. She said she was tired.
A complete unit of meaning containing at least one main clause, beginning with a capital letter and ending with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark. The bell rang.
The grammatical form indicating just one. book, child, woman. Contrast with plural.
A verb that describes a state or condition rather than an action, and is not usually used in the continuous form: know, believe, own, like, seem. I know the answer (not I am knowing).
The person or thing that performs the action of the verb or about which the sentence makes a statement. The children are playing.
A verb mood expressing wishes, suggestions, demands, or hypothetical situations, often with a base-form verb or were. I suggest that he be present.
A clause that cannot stand alone and depends on a main clause, usually introduced by a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun; also called a dependent clause. We left after the film ended.
A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause and links it to a main clause: because, although, if, when, while, since, unless. Call me when you arrive.
A group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or part of speech. happi-ness, quick-ly. See also prefix.
The form of an adjective or adverb used to compare three or more things and show the highest degree, formed with -est or most. the tallest. See also comparative.
A unit of pronunciation containing one vowel sound, with or without surrounding consonants. cat has one syllable; water has two; ba-na-na has three.
The form of a verb that shows the time of an action or state, chiefly present or past, and combined with aspect to express finer time relationships. She plays; she played.
A verb that takes a direct object to complete its meaning. She wrote a letter. Contrast with intransitive verb.
A noun naming something that cannot normally be counted and has no plural form, such as a substance or abstract idea: water, information, advice, furniture. I need some advice (not an advice).
A word that expresses an action, an event, or a state of being. run, think, become, exist. They ran to the bus.
The grammatical category showing whether the subject performs the action (active voice) or receives it (passive voice). The chef cooked the meal / The meal was cooked.
A category into which words are grouped according to how they behave in a sentence: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, determiner, and interjection.
The absence of any article before a noun, common with plural and uncountable nouns used in a general sense. I like music; cats are independent.
